lessons.title: Travelling in the Past

activities.prompt: How did people journey through the world long ago?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ways People Travelled
activities.body: Transport means the ways people travel from place to place. People have always been interested in travelling. Vehicles are things used for travel, such as carts, cars, trains, boats, and ships. In earlier years, there were far fewer vehicles. Long before that, people travelled on foot or used animals. Boats were probably the first transport invented by humans.
keyPoints: People have always been interested in travelling.
People travelled on foot, with animals, and by vehicle.
Boats were probably the first kind of transport invented by humans.
activities.explanation: These are the main travel methods from the lesson.

Therefore, 8 animals are needed for the two carts.

lessons.title: Reading and Writing Large Numbers

activities.prompt: How can commas make really big numbers easier to read?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The TTh Column
activities.body: The place value chart now has a TTh column. TTh stands for ten thousand. Ten Ones make one Ten. Ten Tens make one Hundred. Ten Hundreds make one Thousand. Ten Thousands make Ten Thousand. A comma helps us read large numbers easily. Numbers beyond 10,000 are written like numbers below 9,999. The number 9,123 has 9 Thousands, 1 Hundred, 2 Tens, and 3 Ones.
keyPoints: TTh means ten thousand.
A comma helps us read large numbers.
Large numbers use place value columns.
activities.explanation: TTh means ten thousand.

activities.title: Build a big number

tasks.say: Make one lakh.
tasks.when: crores == 0 and lakhs == 1 and thousands == 0 and ones == 0
tasks.then: 1,00,000 in the Indian system is 100,000: a hundred thousand.

tasks.say: Make ten lakh.
tasks.when: crores == 0 and lakhs == 10 and thousands == 0 and ones == 0
tasks.then: 10,00,000 is 1,000,000: ten lakh is one million.

tasks.say: Make one crore.
tasks.when: crores == 1 and lakhs == 0 and thousands == 0 and ones == 0
tasks.then: 1,00,00,000 is 10,000,000: one crore is ten million.

activities.takeaway: One lakh is a hundred thousand, ten lakh is a million, and one crore is ten million.

activities.title: Compare, Swap, and Round
activities.body: The lesson shows how to compare numbers, swap digits, and round to the nearest ten. A student claimed that 9,990 was greater than 49,014 because 9 was greater than 4. A place value chart can help compare numbers. Interchanging 7 and 4 in 1,478 gives 1,748. The nearest ten of 2,346 is 2,350. Also, 19 and 21 both have nearest ten 20.
keyPoints: A place value chart can help compare numbers.
Interchanging 7 and 4 in 1,478 gives 1,748.
The nearest ten of 2,346 is 2,350.
activities.explanation: Careful comparisons and rounding give clearer results.

Vijay and Suma got the same rounding result, so their rounded answers matched.

lessons.title: Travelling Now and Then

activities.prompt: How has the way people travel changed through the years?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ways of travelling
activities.body: Long ago, travellers used animals for journeys. Bullocks, horses, donkeys, mules and elephants helped them travel. Camels were used in deserts. Today, people use bicycles, motorbikes, cars, buses, trains, ships and aeroplanes. Submarines travel deep underwater, while spacecraft carry people into outer space. Different journeys cover very different distances each hour.
keyPoints: Past travellers used animals, including bullocks, horses, donkeys, mules and elephants.
Camels were used in deserts.
Modern travel includes trains, ships and aeroplanes.
Submarines go under water, and spacecraft carry people to outer space.
activities.explanation: This lesson compares old and new ways to travel.

activities.title: Big numbers and pebble puzzles
activities.body: Large numbers can describe distances from one digit to five digits. A book has around 200 pages, with about 50 words on each page. That gives about 10,000 words altogether. In the pebble game, there are two piles, and each pile has 7 pebbles. A player may choose either pile. The player who takes the last pebble wins. You can also explore digits, differences, and reaching a one-digit number.
keyPoints: Transport distances can have 1 to 5 digits.
A book has about 200 pages and 50 words per page.
Two pebble piles each hold 7 pebbles.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect large numbers with books and pebble puzzles.

activities.title: Build a big number

tasks.say: Make one lakh.
tasks.when: crores == 0 and lakhs == 1 and thousands == 0 and ones == 0
tasks.then: 1,00,000 in the Indian system is 100,000: a hundred thousand.

tasks.say: Make ten lakh.
tasks.when: crores == 0 and lakhs == 10 and thousands == 0 and ones == 0
tasks.then: 10,00,000 is 1,000,000: ten lakh is one million.

tasks.say: Make one crore.
tasks.when: crores == 1 and lakhs == 0 and thousands == 0 and ones == 0
tasks.then: 1,00,00,000 is 10,000,000: one crore is ten million.

activities.takeaway: One lakh is a hundred thousand, ten lakh is a million, and one crore is ten million.
activities.explanation: One lakh is a hundred thousand, ten lakh is a million, and one crore is ten million.

activities.title: Understanding Full and Half Turns
activities.body: A full turn makes a complete circle. A half turn can make a half-moon shape. The minute hand returns to its initial position after a full turn. A giant wheel makes a full turn when it returns to its starting position. Many everyday objects involve turns. Angles arise in situations that involve a turn.
keyPoints: A full turn makes a complete circle.
A half turn can make a half-moon shape.
Turns are involved in many everyday situations.
activities.explanation: Turns can be seen in clocks, wheels, objects and many daily activities.

lessons.title: Quarter Turns and Angles

activities.prompt: What happens when a turn grows from a tiny corner to a wide opening?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Turns and Angles
activities.body: A quarter of a full turn looks like a right angle. A turn smaller than a quarter turn looks acute. A turn larger than a quarter but smaller than a half looks obtuse. Two quarter turns make a straight angle. A paper fan can show different acute and obtuse angles. You can see its turns while keeping one side fixed.
keyPoints: A quarter turn looks like a right angle.
Smaller turns look acute.
Larger turns can look obtuse.
Two quarter turns make a straight angle.
activities.explanation: This lesson helps you name angles from the size of a turn.

activities.prompt: A bus makes 16 quarter turns in the same direction. How many full turns is that?
steps: The bus makes 16 quarter turns.
Four quarter turns make one full turn, so share 16 quarter turns into groups of four.
16 ÷ 4 = 4 full turns.

gen.template: A bus makes {n} quarter turns in the same direction. How many full turns is that?
steps: The bus makes {n} quarter turns.
Four quarter turns make one full turn, so share {n} quarter turns into groups of four.
{n} ÷ {per_full} = {answer} full turns.
gen.hint: Group the quarter turns into groups of four.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: You fold a rectangular paper every 2 cm to make a fan. One side stays fixed. What angles can the fan show?
steps: Keep one side fixed, so the fan's turns can be seen.
Turns under a quarter are acute because they are smaller than right angles.
Turns over a quarter look obtuse because they stay under a half.
So the fan can show different acute and obtuse angles.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose the Angle

A right angle

activities.explanation: A turn smaller than a quarter turn looks acute.

activities.prompt: A path has 5 straight-angle turns. How many right angles do these turns contain altogether?
activities.explanation: There are 5 straight-angle turns. Each straight angle contains 2 right angles. 5 × 2 = 10 right angles.

activities.explanation: The moving side of the fan opens through 3 quarter turns. Each quarter turn is one right angle. The fan shows 3 right-angle turns, so the answer is 3.

why.a straight angle: This mistake treats one turn over a quarter as two quarter turns.

It makes a right angle, not an acute one.
It makes an acute angle because both turns are small.

why.It makes a right angle, not an acute one: This mistake counts only the first quarter turn.

activities.explanation: This is right: two quarter turns make a straight angle.

why.An obtuse angle: This mistake calls a quarter turn larger than a quarter turn.
why.A straight angle: This mistake treats one quarter turn as two quarter turns.

activities.explanation: This is right: a quarter turn looks like a right angle.

It has no acute angle, but two right.

This mistake swaps the right and acute angle counts.
This mistake swaps the obtuse and acute angle counts.
This mistake leaves out the shape's one acute angle.

lessons.title: Making an Angle Measuring Tool

activities.prompt: Can you make a simple tool that helps you measure angles?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How the Tool Is Made
activities.body: This tool uses a folded circle and a straw to show turns. First, fold a circle into eight equal parts. Attach a straw at the centre and mark a starting point. The straw can show an eighth turn. You can also fold the circle again into three equal parts, attach another straw, and cut out one-sixth parts. Paste the finished parts on thicker paper or board.
keyPoints: Fold the circle into eight equal parts.
Attach a straw at the centre.
Cut out one-sixth parts for another exercise.
activities.explanation: These steps will help you make and use your measuring tool.

activities.prompt: A child wants an angle tool that shows an eighth turn. What should the child do?
steps: First, fold a circle into 8 equal parts to make equal-sized parts.
Attach a straw at the centre, because the tool turns from there.
Mark a starting point, so the straw has a clear beginning.
Finally, the straw can show an eighth turn, making an angle tool.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

options: A circle

activities.explanation: Yes, the straw stays at the centre of the circle.

activities.hint: Think of the first way the circle is folded.
activities.explanation: The first fold makes eight equal parts.

activities.hint: Choose the strong, flat material from the lesson.
activities.explanation: The finished parts can be pasted on thicker paper or board.

activities.prompt: A circle is folded into 8 equal parts. A straw is attached at the centre. A starting point is marked. What can the straw show?
options: An eighth turn

why.A third turn: This confuses the straw's eighth turn with a third turn.

lessons.title: Measuring and Drawing Angles

activities.prompt: How can we discover the secret angles hiding in shapes?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Angles, Turns and Tools
activities.body: You may first guess each angle measure. An angle-measuring tool helps you check it. After measuring, call each angle acute, right or obtuse. Sometimes a combination of measures may be needed. You measure each angle in shapes, and write the measures in turns. An arrow can make turns, and angle-measuring tools can verify them. You can draw angles for given turn measures using given lines.
keyPoints: An angle-measuring tool checks a measure.
Measured angles can be acute, right or obtuse.
Given turns can be checked or drawn using lines and tools.
activities.explanation: This joins guessing, checking, naming, and drawing angles.

lessons.title: Clockwise and Anti-clockwise Turns

activities.prompt: Want to discover how to turn and find a new facing direction?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Clockwise and anti-clockwise movement
activities.body: Clock-hand movement is called clockwise movement. The opposite movement is called anti-clockwise movement. You can observe movement while opening a tap, unscrewing a lid, or loosening a nut. The pictured creatures have each made a quarter turn once. The teacher tells children which direction to rotate. Children then complete a table showing the directions they will face.
keyPoints: Clock-hand movement is clockwise movement.
The opposite movement is anti-clockwise movement.
Turns can be observed during everyday actions.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you describe and observe different turns.

activities.prompt: A clock hand makes 2 quarter turns clockwise. How many right angles does it turn through?
steps: The clock hand makes 2 quarter turns clockwise.
Each quarter turn is one right angle, so the number of right angles is the same.
2 = 2, so the answer is 2 right angles.

gen.template: A clock hand makes {turns} quarter turns clockwise. How many right angles does it turn through?
steps: The clock hand makes {turns} quarter turns clockwise.
Each quarter turn is one right angle, so the number of right angles is the same.
{turns} = {answer}, so the answer is {answer} right angles.
gen.hint: Remember that one quarter turn is one right angle.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: A child faces North in a school corridor. The teacher gives two right angles clockwise. Which direction will the child face?
steps: The child starts facing North, so we use North first.
Clockwise follows the clock hands, so we turn in that direction.
Two clockwise right angles from North lead South, so both turns count.
The child therefore finishes facing South.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Match each movement clue with its description.
activities.explanation: Clock hands move clockwise, and the opposite is anti-clockwise. The pictured creatures each make a quarter turn once.

activities.prompt: What is the movement of clock hands called?
options: Clockwise movement
Anti-clockwise movement
Quarter-turn movement
Right-angle movement

activities.title: Choosing the Right Unit
activities.body: Choose suitable units when you measure length. The India Gate is 42 metres high. A handkerchief is 40 centimetres long. A well is 50 metres deep. A mobile phone is 13 centimetres long. An elephant’s trunk is 2 metres long. The gap between shirt buttons is 5 centimetres. Different units have relationships. The double number line helps match measures for the same sari or stole.
keyPoints: Metres and centimetres are units for length, and they have relationships.
The lesson gives measures for objects such as India Gate and a handkerchief.
The double number line matches measures for the same sari or stole.
activities.explanation: These examples help you choose the right unit and practise matching.

activities.prompt: How can tiny marks help us measure lengths more precisely?

activities.title: Meet the Millimetre
activities.body: A centimetre is divided into ten equal parts. Each part is one millimetre, a unit for measuring smaller lengths. So, one centimetre equals ten millimetres. Small marks help us measure smaller lengths more precisely. One hundred centimetres equal one metre.

Each equal part is one millimetre.
One hundred centimetres equal one metre.

activities.prompt: Ready to discover how cloth, thread, roads, and height connect?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Lengths, Costs and References
activities.body: Length and cost can be connected through equal groups. One shirt needs 1 m 80 cm. Twenty shirts need 36 m altogether. Cloth costing ₹100 for 5 m costs ₹20 for 1 m. A double number line can find cloth costs and lengths bought. For estimating heights, use a reference. One foot has 12 inches and equals 30 cm.
keyPoints: Equal groups help us find totals and shares.
A double number line finds costs and lengths.
A reference helps estimate a height.
activities.explanation: Use equal groups, prices and references to work with lengths.

activities.prompt: A tailor has 36 m of cloth. Is this enough for 20 shirts for 10-year-old children?
steps: Each shirt needs 1 m 80 cm, so start with the length for one.
There are twenty shirts, so multiply 1 m 80 cm by 20.
The product is 36 m, which agrees with the given cloth total.
So 36 m is enough because it equals the amount needed for twenty shirts.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does 1 m of this cloth cost?
activities.explanation: Cloth costing ₹100 for 5 m costs ₹20 for 1 m.

activities.hint: Use the thread length given in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put these lengths from shortest to longest.

why.1 shirt: This counts one shirt instead of sharing all the cloth.

why.The mobile phone’s length would match it: Matching measures must represent the same length.

lessons.title: Multiplying in Different Ways

activities.prompt: Can you discover how shapes become products?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Using Shapes and Clues
activities.body: Some puzzles use shapes instead of written numbers. Each shape stands for a number from 1 to 24. A shape that looks the same always has the same number in every problem. The digits 2, 5 and 3 must be placed properly. The product is the multiplication answer. It should be close to 100.
keyPoints: Shapes stand for numbers from 1 to 24
Matching shapes keep the same number
The product should be close to 100
activities.explanation: Use each clue carefully to solve the puzzle.

activities.prompt: A dairy has 3 trays, and each tray has 3 pouches. How many pouches are there altogether?
steps: There are 3 trays.
Each tray has 3 pouches, so multiply 3 by 3.
3 x 3 = 9 pouches.

activities.prompt: A dairy packs butter milk pouches. Children make other groups from them. Why does regrouping keep the same total?
steps: Equal groups are counted by multiplying because every group has the same size.

So 3 groups of 8 show the same total as 8 groups of 3.
Both ways show 24 pouches because 3 × 8 equals 24.

lessons.title: Order of Numbers and Multiplication by 10s and 100s

activities.prompt: Ready to discover what happens when groups and digits move?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different Ways to Arrange Packets
activities.body: Butter packets can be arranged in different ways. Changing the number of groups and group size gives another arrangement. The total number of packets stays the same. Ten times ten is 100. Multiplying by 10 makes a number ten times as large and moves each digit one place left. Multiplying by 100 makes it 100 times as large. Numbers can be multiplied in any order.
keyPoints: Different arrangements can have the same total.
Multiplying by 10 moves each digit one place left.
Numbers can be multiplied in any order.
activities.explanation: Different arrangements can keep the same total.

activities.prompt: Each of 10 boxes contains 3 butter packets. How many butter packets are there in all 10 boxes?
steps: Each box contains 3 butter packets.
We multiply by 10 because there are 10 equal boxes.
The total is 30 butter packets.

gen.hint: Multiply the number of packets in one box by 10.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: Daljeet Kaur arranges 300 butter packets in equal groups. How can she change the arrangement without changing the total?
steps: She can make 3 groups with 100 packets in each group.
This gives 300 packets because 3 times 100 equals 300.
She can make 100 groups with 3 packets in each group.
The total stays 300 because only the groups and group size change.

lessons.title: Many Ways to Multiply

activities.prompt: Can you discover a quicker way to multiply 18 by 5?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different ways to find a product
activities.body: Multiplication can be worked out in more than one way. The product of 18 and 5 is 90. You can halve 18 to find 9, or double 18 to get 36. Doubling 36 gives 72, and adding 18 to 72 gives 90. Another route separates 18 into 8 and 10. Multiplying 8 and 10 by 5 gives 40 and 50.
keyPoints: Different methods can find the same product.
Doubling and adding can reach 90.
Separating 18 into 8 and 10 is another route.
activities.explanation: These methods show different ways to multiply.

activities.prompt: There are 18 boxes with 5 laddoos in each box. How many laddoos are there in all?
steps: There are 18 boxes and 5 laddoos in each box.
Equal groups are multiplied to find the total.
18 x 5 = 90 laddoos.

gen.hint: Count the laddoos in all the equal groups.

Add 40 and 50, because this gives the total of 90.

activities.prompt: How does multiplying by 10 differ from multiplying by 100?
activities.answer: Multiplying a number by 10 makes it 10 times as large and moves each digit one place to the left. Multiplying by 100 makes it 100 times as large and moves each digit two places to the left. The rules use different multipliers and different numbers of places.
points: Multiplying by 10 makes a number 10 times as large.
Multiplying by 10 moves each digit one place to the left.

Multiplying by 100 moves each digit two places to the left.

activities.context: At a school fair, a volunteer needs to work out how many prizes are prepared for 18 groups of 5. One method doubles 18 to 36 and doubles 36 to 72; adding 18 to 72 gives 90, matching the product of 18 and 5. Another method separates 18 into 8 and 10, then multiplies each part by 5 to get 40 and 50. The volunteer also knows that 20 times 5 is 100 and 2 times 5 is 10.

why.54: 54 comes from six times nine, not the doubling steps.

activities.context: At a school fair, a volunteer needs to work out how many prizes are prepared for 18 groups of 5. activities.prompt: Explain why adding 18 to 72 completes the doubling method for multiplying 18 by 5.
activities.answer: The doubling steps reach 36 and then 72. The facts say that adding 18 to 72 gives 90, and that the product of 18 and 5 is 90. Therefore, adding 18 after the doubling steps completes the same multiplication in a different way.
points: Doubles 18 to 36.
Doubles 36 to 72.
Adds 18 to 72.
Gets the same result as 18 times 5.

lessons.title: Tiling and Tessellation

activities.prompt: Can regular shapes cover a surface without leaving any gaps?

activities.title: What is tessellation?
activities.body: Tessellation means tiles cover a region without gaps. Tiles may have same or different shapes. A pentagon has five sides. If all sides are equal, it is a regular pentagon. Regular pentagons leave gaps, so they do not tessellate. Regular triangles fit around a point without gaps or overlaps. Equilateral triangles tessellate. A tessellating pattern may use different shapes. Regular octagons have eight equal sides but do not tessellate.
keyPoints: Regular pentagons leave gaps.
Equilateral triangles tessellate.
Tessellations may use different shapes.
activities.explanation: Notice gaps, overlaps, and equal sides.

Equilateral triangles leave no gaps, so they tessellate.
The child should choose equilateral triangles for the floor.

activities.title: Connected Number Facts
activities.body: Multiplication and division are connected. Five groups of seven make thirty-five. This is also seven groups of five. Dividing thirty-five by five gives seven. Dividing thirty-five by seven gives five. The dividend is the number being divided. The divisor is the number dividing it. The quotient is the answer. A letter helps us name each part.
keyPoints: Five times seven equals thirty-five.
Dividing thirty-five by five gives seven.
The dividend equals the divisor multiplied by the quotient.

Divide and check your answer.

lessons.title: Making a Windmill Firki

activities.prompt: Can you turn a simple square of paper into a spinning windmill?

activities.title: How to make a firki
activities.body: Make a firki by starting with square paper. Fold it diagonally to make two triangles. Open it, then fold the other way to make two more triangles. When you open it, you see an X shape. Cut along the X’s four lines, stopping halfway to the centre. Fold the corners towards the centre, then push a pin through. Keep the pin not too tight, then check whether it spins in the wind.

Cut the X lines and fold the corners towards the centre.
Push a pin through and check the windmill in the wind.

Check it in the wind, because a finished firki should spin there.

activities.title: Checking a Turned Shape
activities.body: Rotational symmetry means a shape looks the same after it is turned. A dot helps keep track of a letter's orientation. You can cut out a letter and fix its centre point with a nail. Use tracing paper to check whether a turned letter looks the same. The letter H looks the same after a half-turn, so it has rotational symmetry. A firki has rotational symmetry.
keyPoints: A dot helps track a letter's orientation.
A nail fixes the letter's centre point.
Tracing paper checks a turned letter.
activities.explanation: Good start! These tools help you check rotational symmetry.

activities.takeaway: The number of times a shape looks the same in one full turn is its order of rotational symmetry.

activities.context: Prem and Manu are preparing Happy Birthday letter cutouts for a wall. They choose A and H because reflection symmetry helps them make the letters. activities.prompt: Why does opening the paper show the complete letter A?

activities.context: Preetha and Adrit’s grandmother made a quilt cover from old clothes. Now she wants to decorate the quilt cover with lace. The lace must cover the entire border of the quilt. activities.prompt: Why must the lace cover the entire border of the quilt?
options: To cover every part of the quilt’s border
To cover the centre of the quilt
To make the two laces the same colour
To change the perimeter of the quilt

why.To cover the centre of the quilt: Covering the centre would not follow the instruction.
why.To make the two laces the same colour: The two laces are meant to have different colours.
why.To change the perimeter of the quilt: Nothing in the case says the border length will change.

activities.explanation: The case says the lace must cover the whole border.

activities.context: Preetha and Adrit’s grandmother made a quilt cover from old clothes. Now she wants to decorate the quilt cover with lace. The lace must cover the entire border of the quilt. The centre of the quilt
The number of colours used

why.The colour of one lace: A colour does not measure border length.
why.The centre of the quilt: The lace is for the border, not the centre.
why.The number of colours used: The number of colours does not give the border length.

activities.explanation: Perimeter means the length of a shape’s border.

activities.prompt: Explain why the perimeter is the same as the border length.
activities.answer: The perimeter is the length of a shape’s border. The border of the quilt is the part that the lace must cover completely. Therefore, the perimeter gives the total length of lace needed to cover the whole quilt border.
points: Perimeter means border length.
The lace covers the quilt’s border.
The perimeter gives the total length needed.
The centre is not part of the lace border.

activities.context: Grandmother is making a rug with square patches. The picture shows the rug she is making. Preetha and Adrit are trying to cover their table with different shapes. Preetha covered the table with triangles and circles, while Adrit covered it with squares and rectangles. An area is the region covered by triangles, squares, or rectangles. To find an area, the region is filled with tiling shapes that fit together without gaps or overlaps.
activities.prompt: Preetha shifts a triangle so that it covers part of another triangle. What has happened to the tiling?
options: The shapes now overlap, so they no longer meet the tiling rule.
The shapes still form a tiling because overlapping does not matter.
An uncovered gap has been created even though the triangles overlap.
The area has become larger because the overlapping part is covered twice.

why.The shapes still form a tiling because o: The tiling rule does not allow overlaps.
why.An uncovered gap has been created even t: Overlapping triangles do not automatically create a gap.
why.The area has become larger because the o: Covering part twice does not make the covered region larger.

activities.explanation: Overlapping means the tiles do not fit correctly.

activities.context: Grandmother is making a rug with square patches. The picture shows the rug she is making. Preetha and Adrit are trying to cover their table with different shapes. Preetha covered the table with triangles and circles, while Adrit covered it with squares and rectangles. An area is the region covered by triangles, squares, or rectangles. To find an area, the region is filled with tiling shapes that fit together without gaps or overlaps.
activities.prompt: Adrit wants his square and rectangle tiles to give an exact area. What should he do before finding the area?
options: Fill the table region so the tiles fit with neither uncovered space nor double covering.
Leave spaces between the tiles because gaps do not affect the result.
Place the tiles over one another so every part seems covered.
Use only one tile shape even when it cannot fill the whole region.

why.Leave spaces between the tiles because g: Leaving gaps would leave part of the region uncovered.
why.Place the tiles over one another so ever: Overlapping tiles would cover some parts again.
why.Use only one tile shape even when it can: Using a shape that cannot fill the region would leave spaces.

activities.explanation: An exact tiling covers the region without gaps or overlaps.

activities.prompt: Explain why tiling shapes must fit together without gaps or overlaps.
activities.answer: An exact tiling needs every part of the region covered once. If tiles overlap, some space is covered again, and if there are gaps, some space is not covered. Either problem means the shapes do not fit together correctly, so the tiling cannot be used to find the area reliably.
points: The whole region must be covered.
Gaps leave part of the region uncovered.
Overlaps cover some space again.
Either problem breaks the tiling rule.

activities.prompt: Explain why multiplying the number of rows by the number of columns gives the area of a rectangle tiled by unit squares.

The product gives the number of unit squares.
The number of unit squares gives the area.

lessons.title: Elapsed Time and Painting Times

activities.prompt: Can you discover how long each child took to paint?

activities.title: What is elapsed time?
activities.body: Elapsed time is the time that passes between a start and an end. It helps you answer questions about practice and painting. You can find it using clock times. The lesson shows several examples. It asks when Raghav started and finished practising Yoga. It also compares how long Raghav, Rani, and Ritu took to paint. You will find the longest and shortest painting times.
keyPoints: Elapsed time is the time between a start and an end.
The lesson asks when Raghav started and finished practising Yoga.
Longer painting times can be compared with shorter painting times.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you compare start times, finish times, and painting durations.

activities.prompt: Raghav, Rani, and Ritu start painting one picture together. Who will finish last?
steps: Compare the times, because they all started painting together.
Two hours 10 minutes is longer than Raghav's 1 hour 20 minutes.
One hour 35 minutes is shorter than Raghav's 1 hour 20 minutes.
Rani will finish last, because 2 hours 10 minutes is longest.

activities.title: Estimate Short Times
activities.body: Short times can be estimated by thinking about familiar actions. Try blinking your eyes, switching a light on and off, counting from 1 to 20. lessons.title: The Mystery Box

activities.title: Meet the Mystery Box
activities.body: The mystery box multiplies a number before the number comes out. The multipliers used here are 1, 2 and 4. These are factors of every output number, so they are common factors. The four outputs are 28, 36, 48 and 72. Each output is a multiple of 1, 2 and 4. An array shows the factors of a number.
keyPoints: The box multiplies each number.
The multipliers are 1, 2 and 4.
Each output is a multiple of 1, 2 and 4.
activities.explanation: The mystery box shows how multiplication and factors work together.

steps: The number going into the mystery box is 4.
The mystery box multiplies 4 by 3.
The number that comes out is 12.

The box multiplies 12 by 4, because that is the chosen multiplier.

activities.body: The lesson shows pairs of factors in an array. It gives 3 and 5 as one factor pair of 15. For 12, the factor pairs are 1 and 12, 2 and 6, and 3 and 4. Multiplying two or more factors gives a multiple. The mystery box uses the multipliers 1, 2 and 4.

12 has three factor pairs.
Multiplying factors gives a multiple.

activities.body: Factors divide 12 completely. The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. A rabbit jumps 4 spaces each time, while a frog jumps 3 spaces each time. Both start from 0. A number touched by both animals is called a common multiple. The first common multiple of 3 and 4 is 12.

tasks.then: 24 makes 4 rectangles: 1 x 24, 2 x 12, 3 x 8 and 4 x 6.

tasks.say: Find a prime number bigger than 20.
tasks.then: It makes only one long row, so it has just two factors: it is prime.

tasks.say: Find the number up to 40 with 9 factors.
tasks.then: 36 has 9 factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. Square numbers have an odd number of factors.

activities.takeaway: Every rectangle a number can make is a factor pair; a prime can only make one long row.
activities.explanation: Every rectangle a number can make is a factor pair; a prime can only make one long row.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a factor and a multiple.
activities.answer: A factor pairs with another factor to make a number. A multiple is made by multiplying a number. For example, 3 and 5 form a factor pair of 15. Also, 1, 2 and 4 are common factors of the outputs because each output is a multiple of each of them.

Explains that multiples are made by multiplication.

why.3 and 4 are multiples of 12: This reverses the correct multiple relationship.
why.Only the frog can land on 12: The rabbit can also reach 12 by jumping 4 each time.

activities.explanation: 12 is a multiple of all its factors, including 3 and 4.

They flew from North to South without resting.
They returned home with their mother.
Facing the rising Sun helps find directions.
activities.explanation: The chicks' journey shows different directions and one way to find them.

Therefore, the child can find a direction by facing the rising Sun.

chapters.summary: In this chapter: watching tv data; making pictographs; recording a day and a bar graph; comparing index-finger lengths.

lessons.title: Watching TV data

activities.prompt: Which amount of TV watching is most common among our friends?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Collecting TV data
activities.body: Samaira and Kabir collected information about TV watching from 35 friends. They wrote the information in a notebook. Their table shows how many hours children watch TV. It also shows the number of children for each time. The table includes one hour, two hours, and more than two hours. You can compare the table to learn what this group watches.
keyPoints: They collected data from 35 friends.
They recorded the information in a notebook.
The table shows TV hours and the number of children.
activities.explanation: This data helps you compare how much TV the children watch.

activities.prompt: Kabir says fewer children watch for two hours than half an hour. Can Samaira use the table to check him?
steps: The table gives group sizes, so it can check Kabir's claim.
Compare the two-hour and half-hour groups, because Kabir claims one is smaller.
More children watch for two hours, so Kabir's claim is wrong.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Reading the TV table
activities.body: A data table keeps related information together. In this table, one part shows the number of TV hours. Another part shows the number of children. You can compare the information for different times. The two-hour group has more children than the half-hour group.
keyPoints: One part shows the number of TV hours.
Another part shows the number of children.
You can compare the groups using the table.
activities.explanation: Comparing the table helps you find which group has more children.

activities.prompt: Where did Samaira and Kabir record the information?
options: A shopping list
A notebook
A diary
A poster
activities.explanation: They recorded the information in a notebook.

activities.prompt: They collected data from ______ friends.
activities.hint: Use the number of children they asked.
activities.explanation: Samaira and Kabir collected data from 35 friends.

activities.prompt: Samaira and Kabir collected data from 35 friends.
activities.explanation: They collected information about TV watching from 35 friends.

activities.prompt: Match each TV time to the children it describes.

activities.prompt: What information does the table give?
options: The TV hours and child numbers

The child numbers without TV hours
The child names and TV hours
activities.explanation: The table records both the number of TV hours and the number of children.

activities.prompt: Which comparison about the table is true?
options: Two hours had fewer children than half an hour.
Half an hour had more children than two hours.
Two hours had more children than half an hour.
The table showed hours but no child numbers.
activities.explanation: More children watch TV for two hours than for half an hour.

activities.prompt: Samaira and Kabir's table shows watching hours and numbers of children. A class wants a similar table. What should each row show?
options: The number of children for each watching time.
The name of each child for each watching time.
The number of children for each friend's hobby.
The number of children for each watching place.

why.The name of each child for each watching: The table counts children rather than recording their names.
why.The number of children for each friend's: A hobby is not the watching time recorded by the table.
why.The number of children for each watching: A watching place is not a watching time.

activities.explanation: Each row pairs a watching time with the number of children.

activities.prompt: The data compares two-hour and half-hour groups. Kabir says the two-hour group is smaller. Is Kabir right?
options: No, the two-hour group has more children.
Yes, the two-hour group has fewer children.
No, both groups have exactly the same size.
Yes, the half-hour group has no children.

why.Yes, the two-hour group has fewer childr: This claim says the opposite of what the data shows.
why.No, both groups have exactly the same si: The two groups have different sizes, so their numbers are not equal.
why.Yes, the half-hour group has no children: The half-hour group has children, so it is not empty.

activities.explanation: The data shows more children watch for two hours than half an hour.

activities.prompt: A child moves from the half-hour group to the two-hour group. The two-hour group was larger before. What happens?
options: The two-hour group gets farther ahead of the half-hour group.
The half-hour group gets farther ahead of the two-hour group.
The two-hour group becomes the same size as the half-hour group.
The two-hour group becomes smaller than the half-hour group.

why.The half-hour group gets farther ahead o: This reverses the change caused by moving the child.
why.The two-hour group becomes the same size: The two-hour group grows, so its lead grows too.
why.The two-hour group becomes smaller than: The two-hour group grows, so it does not become smaller.

activities.explanation: Moving one child increases the larger group and decreases the smaller group.

activities.prompt: Samaira and Kabir asked 35 friends and wrote their answers. Why record those answers in a notebook?
options: To keep the information needed for their data table.
To change each friend's answer into a different answer.
To show that every friend watched TV for two hours.
To remove the need to count children by watching time.

why.To change each friend's answer into a di: Recording answers does not change what the friends said.
why.To show that every friend watched TV for: The table compares groups rather than showing one shared time.
why.To remove the need to count children by: The table needs the numbers of children in each time group.

activities.explanation: The notebook keeps the answers for making the data table.

activities.context: Samaira and Kabir decided to act like reporters and collect information from their friends. They gathered details from 35 friends and wrote them in a notebook. Their table shows both the number of hours spent watching TV and the number of children in each group. It includes half an hour, one hour, two hours, and more than two hours. Samaira noticed that more children watch TV for two hours than for half an hour.
activities.prompt: If the two-hour count fell while the half-hour count rose, what would happen to the difference between the two-hour count and the half-hour count?
options: It would become smaller.
It would become larger.
It would stay the same.
It would always become zero.

A rising half-hour count also reduces the difference.
Because both counts change, the difference cannot stay the same.
There is not enough information to show that the difference must become zero.

activities.explanation: A falling two-hour count reduces the difference.

activities.context: Samaira and Kabir decided to act like reporters and collect information from their friends. They gathered details from 35 friends and wrote them in a notebook. Their table shows both the number of hours spent watching TV and the number of children in each group. It includes half an hour, one hour, two hours, and more than two hours. Samaira noticed that more children watch TV for two hours than for half an hour.
activities.prompt: Kabir wants to check that all the collected friends are represented in the table. What should he do?
options: Add the child counts from every group and check for a total of 35.
Add the viewing hours from every group and check for a total of 35.
Use only the one-hour and two-hour child counts and check for a total of 35.
Compare the two-hour and half-hour child counts and check for a total of 35.

why.Add the viewing hours from every group a: Adding viewing hours does not count the children.
why.Use only the one-hour and two-hour child: Using only some groups would leave out other children.
why.Compare the two-hour and half-hour child: Comparing two groups does not include every child in the total.

activities.explanation: All the groups together should represent the 35 collected friends.

activities.prompt: Explain how the table can show that more children watch TV for two hours than for half an hour.
activities.answer: The table lists the number of children for each amount of TV watching. To make the comparison, Samaira and Kabir can look at the child count for two hours and the child count for half an hour. The two-hour count is greater, so more children are in that group.
points: The table gives a number of children for each viewing time.
The two relevant counts are for two hours and half an hour.
The two-hour child count is greater.
The greater count explains the observation.

activities.context: Joseph Uncle takes stock of his play items a week before the summer break. His shop contains toys, board games and sports items, and there are too many items of each kind to show every one in a picture. Dipesh suggests using icons, with one icon for every five items of each kind, and records the stock on a scale. Deepti records two-wheelers on three different days, using one icon to show three two-wheelers.
activities.prompt: How should Dipesh represent five toys in the pictograph?
options: With one icon standing for the whole group
With five separate icons, one for each toy
With one icon for every toy, plus one extra
Without an icon, because a picture is needed for every item

why.With five separate icons, one for each t: Five separate icons would ignore the scale.
why.With one icon for every toy, plus one ex: The extra icon is not part of the stated scale.
why.Without an icon, because a picture is ne: No icon would ignore the icon method.

activities.explanation: Correct: the scale groups five items under one icon.

activities.context: Joseph Uncle takes stock of his play items a week before the summer break. His shop contains toys, board games and sports items, and there are too many items of each kind to show every one in a picture. Dipesh suggests using icons, with one icon for every five items of each kind, and records the stock on a scale. activities.prompt: Why is Dipesh using a scale helpful when recording the shop's items?
options: It allows the large stock to be shown with fewer icons.
It requires a separate picture for every item.
It means the two-wheelers should not be recorded.
It means only one kind of play item can be included.

why.It requires a separate picture for every: The method does not require a picture for every item.
why.It means the two-wheelers should not be: Two-wheelers are still included in the record.
why.It means only one kind of play item can: The scale can be used for each kind of item.

activities.explanation: Correct: a scale records large numbers with fewer icons.

activities.prompt: Explain why a scale is useful when Dipesh records the shop's play items.
activities.answer: A scale is useful because there are too many items of each kind to draw separately. Dipesh can group every five items under one icon. This reduces the number of pictures needed while still showing the stock of toys, board games and sports items.
points: There are too many items of each kind.
One icon represents five items.
The scale reduces the number of pictures needed.
Toys, board games and sports items can all be recorded.

activities.context: Raman and Sheela decided to record how they spent their day. Raman put his daily routine in a table, including sleeping, school, studying, eating, playing and other activities. Sheela recorded her routine with bars. Her chart had a vertical line showing hours, a horizontal base for the activities, and a vertical bar for each activity. Together, their records showed how their time was spent.
activities.prompt: Sheela recorded eating and playing. What should her chart contain for each activity?
options: A separate vertical bar showing the hours spent on that activity
One horizontal bar shared by eating and playing
A vertical bar for eating but no bar for playing
A horizontal bar for each activity instead of a vertical bar

why.One horizontal bar shared by eating and: A shared bar would not show each activity separately.
why.A horizontal bar for each activity inste: The hours must be shown with vertical bars.

activities.explanation: Each recorded activity needs its own vertical bar.

activities.context: Raman and Sheela decided to record how they spent their day. Raman put his daily routine in a table, including sleeping, school, studying, eating, playing and other activities. Sheela recorded her routine with bars. Her chart had a vertical line showing hours, a horizontal base for the activities, and a vertical bar for each activity. Together, their records showed how their time was spent.
activities.prompt: Raman wants to record a complete daily routine. What units should he use for the time spent on each activity?
options: Both hours and minutes
Hours only
Minutes only
Activity names only

why.Hours only: Hours alone do not show the complete recorded routine in the required form.
why.Minutes only: Minutes alone do not show the complete recorded routine in the required form.
why.Activity names only: Activity names do not record how much time was spent.

activities.explanation: A daily routine can be recorded using both hours and minutes.

activities.prompt: Why do Raman's table and Sheela's bar graph record daily routines in different ways?
activities.answer: Raman's table records the activities and the time spent on them. Sheela's graph uses a horizontal base for the different activities and vertical bars to show the number of hours spent. Both methods show how time was spent during each person's day.
points: Raman uses a table.
Sheela uses vertical bars.
The base identifies the activities.
Both records show time spent.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Why should all the paper strips have the same width?
activities.answer: They should all have the same width because the graph compares index-finger lengths. If the widths were different, the strips would not provide a fair way to show which index finger is longest. The same width keeps the comparison consistent.
points: The graph compares index-finger lengths.
Different widths would not give a fair comparison.
The same width keeps the comparison consistent.

activities.context: Rani stays in a residential school. In the dining hall, she sees a graph showing which food item had the highest and least wastage, the total food wastage for the days, and the number of children the food could feed. The food is paired with days: sandwich on Monday, paratha on Tuesday, khichdi on Wednesday, puri-sabzi on Thursday, and idli-sambar with Friday. When Rani reads the graph, she is shocked by how much food is wasted.
activities.prompt: The graph includes one kilogram of sandwich waste for Monday. What does this tell Rani about children?
options: That kilogram could feed three children.
That kilogram could feed one child.
That kilogram could feed four children.
That kilogram could not feed any children.

This incorrectly uses one child instead of three.
This changes the stated feeding rate.
why.That kilogram could not feed any childre: This ignores the connection between wasted food and children.

activities.explanation: Correct: one kilogram of food waste can feed three children.

activities.context: Rani stays in a residential school. In the dining hall, she sees a graph showing which food item had the highest and least wastage, the total food wastage for the days, and the number of children the food could feed. The food is paired with days: sandwich on Monday, paratha on Tuesday, khichdi on Wednesday, puri-sabzi on Thursday, and idli-sambar with Friday. activities.prompt: The graph shows sandwich had the highest wastage and idli-sambar had the least wastage. What can Rani conclude?
options: More children could be fed using sandwich waste than idli-sambar waste.
Fewer children could be fed using sandwich waste than idli-sambar waste.
The same number of children could be fed using either waste.
More children could be fed using idli-sambar waste than sandwich waste.

why.Fewer children could be fed using sandwi: This reverses the graph's highest and least information.
why.The same number of children could be fed: This assumes different food wastes feed equal numbers of children.
why.More children could be fed using idli-sa: This treats the least-wasted food as having more impact.

activities.explanation: Correct: the highest wastage could feed more children than the least wastage.

activities.context: Rani stays in a residential school. In the dining hall, she sees a graph showing which food item had the highest and least wastage, the total food wastage for the days, and the number of children the food could feed. why.Use only the total wastage and ignore th: This ignores the graph's information about individual foods.

activities.explanation: Correct: reducing the highest wastage tackles the greatest amount shown.

Explains the link between wasted food and children.

activities.context: During a class picture review, all the girls are wearing glasses, and more boys than girls are holding books. More children are holding books than are wearing caps. Some children wear both glasses and caps, while ten children wear caps on their heads. More than half of the children wear glasses. The picture compares boys wearing glasses with girls wearing glasses and shows that no child has all three items: a cap, a book and a backpack.
activities.prompt: A child who is wearing both glasses and a cap takes off the cap. Which change must happen?
options: The number of children wearing caps decreases by one.
The number of children wearing glasses decreases by one.
The number of children holding books decreases by one.
The number of children wearing both glasses and caps increases by one.

why.The number of children wearing glasses d: The child keeps wearing glasses, so that number does not change.
why.The number of children holding books dec: No book was removed, so the book-holding number does not change.
why.The number of children wearing both glas: The child is no longer wearing both glasses and a cap.

activities.explanation: Taking off a cap reduces the number wearing caps by one.

activities.context: During a class picture review, all the girls are wearing glasses, and more boys than girls are holding books. More children are holding books than are wearing caps. activities.prompt: A child wearing a cap and holding a book puts the book down. Which change must happen?
options: The number of children holding books decreases by one.
The number of children holding books increases by one.
The number of children wearing caps decreases by one.
The number of children wearing both glasses and caps decreases by one.

why.The number of children holding books inc: The child had already been holding the book.
why.The number of children wearing caps decr: The cap remains on the child's head.
why.The number of children wearing both glas: A child with a cap and a book does not also have glasses.

activities.explanation: Putting down the book reduces the number holding books by one.

More than half of the children have glasses.
More boys than girls are holding books.
The number of children holding books is greater than the number wearing caps.

why.More than half of the children have glas: Removing one pair of glasses does not necessarily make this statement false.
The change does not affect which group is holding more books.
why.The number of children holding books is: The change does not affect the comparison between book holders and cap wearers.
